lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat foundational documents only as artefacts and ignore craft.
lessons.real_world_hook: Annotating the Declaration of Independence for parallel structure.

lessons.lesson_title: Evaluate reasoning in seminal texts
lessons.learning_objective: I can evaluate reasoning in a seminal U.S. text including the application of constitutional principles.
lessons.key_concepts: Legal reasoning basics; principles in argument.
lessons.key_vocabulary: constitutional, principle, legal reasoning, evaluate, premise
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students judge reasoning by whether the conclusion matches their values.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a SCOTUS dissent excerpt and naming its reasoning steps.

lessons.lesson_title: Write argument with valid reasoning
lessons.learning_objective: I can write an argument essay with valid reasoning and relevant, sufficient evidence.
lessons.key_concepts: Reasoning chain; relevance; sufficiency.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students offer one example as if it proves a general claim.
lessons.real_world_hook: Pitching a column on early American identity for a school history magazine.

lessons.lesson_title: Resolve complex or contested usage
lessons.learning_objective: I can resolve a contested usage issue using a style guide.
lessons.key_concepts: Style guides as authority; contested vs settled usage.
lessons.key_vocabulary: contested, style guide, usage, authority, resolve
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students argue from feel without consulting a style guide.
lessons.real_world_hook: Settling a Slack debate about whether to write data is or data are.

lessons.lesson_title: Initiate discussion on foundational texts
lessons.learning_objective: I can initiate and probe discussion on a foundational text with text-based questions.
lessons.key_concepts: Probing questions; building chains of reasoning.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students ask broad opinion questions instead of text-anchored ones.
lessons.real_world_hook: Hosting a class discussion in the style of a Philosophize This episode.

lessons.lesson_title: Apply academic vocabulary at CCR level
lessons.learning_objective: I can use academic vocabulary precisely in an analytic essay on a Colonial text.
lessons.key_concepts: Tier 2 vocabulary at CCR level; precision over inflation.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students use Latinate verbs whose meaning they do not quite know.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a draft for precise academic verbs the way a research editor would.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze impact of author's choices on a story
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse the impact of an author's choices about elements of a Romantic novel.
lessons.key_concepts: Author choices; effect on theme; coherence of devices.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students confuse plot summary with analysis of authorial choice.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing Hawthorne's symbol choices the way a literary podcast unpacks decisions.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze figurative and connotative meaning
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse the impact of figurative and connotative meanings on tone in a Romantic poem.
lessons.key_concepts: Figurative; connotation; tone; cumulative.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students label devices without showing impact on tone.
lessons.real_world_hook: Annotating an Emerson essay for connotative weight.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze structure choices contributing to meaning
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how the structure of specific parts of a Romantic novel contributes to overall meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Local structure; chapter design; sequencing.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students consider only overall plot structure, not local design.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing chapter design the way a writer's room plans an episode arc.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate knowledge of foundational American works
lessons.learning_objective: I can compare two foundational American texts on a shared theme.
lessons.key_concepts: Foundational works; comparative analysis; theme.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students compare biographies of authors instead of the texts themselves.
lessons.real_world_hook: Pairing Emerson's Self-Reliance with a current self-help podcast for contrast.

lessons.lesson_title: Write literary analysis on symbol and theme
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a literary analysis on symbol and theme in The Scarlet Letter.
lessons.key_concepts: Symbol analysis; theme integration; controlling claim.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students list symbols and stop without showing meaning.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a piece pitched to an undergraduate literature journal.

lessons.lesson_title: Use varied syntax for effect
lessons.learning_objective: I can vary syntax for effect, including cumulative, periodic, and balanced sentences.
lessons.key_concepts: Sentence types as rhetorical choices.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students default to short subject-verb-object sentences in all analysis.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a TED-style talk for varied sentence rhythm.

lessons.lesson_title: Evaluate effectiveness of a text's structure
lessons.learning_objective: I can evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses to make a point clear and convincing.
lessons.key_concepts: Structure as choice; effectiveness; counterfactual structures.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rate structure by whether they personally enjoyed reading.
lessons.real_world_hook: Auditing a podcast script for structural effectiveness.

lessons.lesson_title: Synthesise multiple sources for argument
lessons.learning_objective: I can synthesise multiple sources on a topic to support an argument.
lessons.key_concepts: Synthesis; source integration; controlling claim.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students stack sources without integrating them.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a feature like a New Yorker Talk of the Town item.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze point of view including irony
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse a case in which point of view requires distinguishing what is directly stated from what is meant.
lessons.key_concepts: Verbal irony; satire; understatement.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students take ironic statements at face value.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a chapter of Huck Finn and a satirical newsletter for layered voice.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze a complex set of ideas in informational text
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse a complex set of ideas in a piece of literary nonfiction.
lessons.key_concepts: Complex argument; interaction of ideas.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students simplify a layered argument into a single thesis.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a James Baldwin essay and mapping its layered claims.

lessons.lesson_title: Determine refined meaning of a key term
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine how the meaning of a key term is refined over the course of a text.
lessons.key_concepts: Key term tracking; redefinition; semantic shift.
lessons.key_vocabulary: key term, refine, shift, redefine, track
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume a key term means the same thing throughout an essay.
lessons.real_world_hook: Tracking the word freedom across a Frederick Douglass speech.

lessons.lesson_title: Determine effective rhetoric in nonfiction
lessons.learning_objective: I can determine an author's point of view in which the rhetoric is particularly effective.
lessons.key_concepts: Effective rhetoric; stance; ethos through diction.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students declare rhetoric effective because they agreed with the conclusion.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing two op-eds on the same topic for effective rhetoric.

lessons.lesson_title: Write argument bridging literature and current issue
lessons.learning_objective: I can write an argument essay using literature to support a position on a current issue.
lessons.key_concepts: Bridge essay; controlling claim; counterclaim.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students argue about the text only or about the issue only.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing an essay that could appear in a school's social issues issue of the magazine.

lessons.lesson_title: Evaluate speaker's evidence and rhetoric
lessons.learning_objective: I can evaluate a speaker's reasoning, evidence, and rhetoric in a recorded address.
lessons.key_concepts: Spoken evaluation; bias detection; structure.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rate addresses by personal style alone.
lessons.real_world_hook: Annotating a current congressional hearing clip for reasoning and rhetoric.

lessons.lesson_title: Use signal phrases for source integration
lessons.learning_objective: I can integrate sources using signal phrases that include credentials, stance, and context.
lessons.key_concepts: Signal phrase craft; ethical attribution.
lessons.key_vocabulary: signal phrase, credential, stance, context, attribute
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students drop quotes with author tags only and no context.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a longform article so each source feels properly introduced.

lessons.lesson_title: Conduct a structured academic seminar
lessons.learning_objective: I can lead a structured academic seminar with text-based evidence and follow up on peer claims.
lessons.key_concepts: Seminar leadership; chain of reasoning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: lead, structured, evidence, chain, follow up
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students dominate when leading and stop building chains of reasoning.
lessons.real_world_hook: Leading a seminar in the style of a public radio panel show.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze how an author's choices develop characters
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how an author's choices develop and relate elements of a modern American novel.
lessons.key_concepts: Modernist choices; character relations; theme.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students analyse characters in isolation rather than their relations.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing relationships in a Toni Morrison chapter.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze multiple interpretations of a text
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse multiple interpretations of a story, drama, or poem.
lessons.key_concepts: Multiple interpretations; performance and reading; production.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students declare one interpretation correct without analysis.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing two staged versions of a contemporary play streamed online.

lessons.lesson_title: Integrate multiple sources of information across media
lessons.learning_objective: I can integrate multiple sources of information in different media to address a question.
lessons.key_concepts: Cross-media integration; source synthesis.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students summarise each source separately and never bring them together.
lessons.real_world_hook: Researching a topic with text, audio, data, and image sources.

lessons.lesson_title: Conduct sustained research and synthesise
lessons.learning_objective: I can conduct a sustained research project that synthesises multiple sources on a subject.
lessons.key_concepts: Sustained research; depth; synthesis.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat sustained research as longer short research.
lessons.real_world_hook: Producing research like a midlength feature for a magazine.

lessons.lesson_title: Write a research paper with controlling idea
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a research paper with a strong controlling idea and disciplined source use.
lessons.key_concepts: Controlling idea; discipline of evidence; cohesion.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students paste source content with no controlling idea.
lessons.real_world_hook: Submitting a piece like a feature for a college-style student paper.

lessons.lesson_title: Write a college admissions essay
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a personal essay of about 650 words that meets a Common App style prompt.
lessons.key_concepts: College essay structure; voice; reflection.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students try to sound impressive instead of specific.
lessons.real_world_hook: Drafting a Common App-style essay for a real prompt.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate command of conventions
lessons.learning_objective: I can demonstrate command of conventions of capitalisation, punctuation, and spelling for academic writing.
lessons.key_concepts: Editing for conventions; hyphenation; spelling.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rely on autocorrect for hyphenation rules.
lessons.real_world_hook: Submitting copy as a student journalist would for a final issue.

lessons.lesson_title: Present research with strategic media
lessons.learning_objective: I can present research with strategic digital media that supports findings and reasoning.
lessons.key_concepts: Strategic media; data viz; reasoning support.
lessons.key_vocabulary: strategic, data viz, support, reasoning, findings
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students put their entire paper on slides and read it.
lessons.real_world_hook: Presenting like a podcaster doing a live event.

lessons.lesson_title: Cite evidence including uncertainty in epic poetry
lessons.learning_objective: I can cite strong evidence in an epic and name where the text leaves meaning uncertain.
lessons.key_concepts: Strong evidence in archaic verse; ambiguity.
lessons.prerequisites: Citing strong evidence in modern texts.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assume archaic verse is simply old, not deliberately ambiguous.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading a Beowulf passage and naming what remains uncertain about Grendel.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze figurative meaning in Old and Middle English
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse figurative meaning in a passage of Beowulf or a Canterbury Tale.
lessons.key_concepts: Kennings; alliterative verse; Middle English vocabulary.
lessons.prerequisites: Analysing figurative meaning in modern poetry.
lessons.key_vocabulary: kenning, alliterative, Middle English, figurative, archaic
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students try to translate every word literally without studying its function.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a kenning to a modern compound nickname in a podcast.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze structure of a frame narrative
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how a frame narrative shapes meaning in the Canterbury Tales.
lessons.key_concepts: Frame narrative; embedded story; structural irony.
lessons.key_vocabulary: frame, embedded, structural irony, layered, narrator
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat the General Prologue and the Tales as if they share one voice.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing Chaucer's frame to a podcast host introducing each guest.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate knowledge of foundational British works
lessons.learning_objective: I can demonstrate knowledge of foundational works in the British tradition.
lessons.key_concepts: Foundational British texts; chronology; influence.
lessons.prerequisites: Demonstrating knowledge of foundational American works.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat all old British texts as one period.
lessons.real_world_hook: Building a class timeline of British literature for a course blog.

lessons.lesson_title: Write literary analysis on heroic code or frame
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a literary analysis essay on the heroic code or on Chaucer's frame.
lessons.key_concepts: Analytic claim about craft; integration of archaic evidence.
lessons.key_vocabulary: heroic code, frame, claim, integrate, analyse
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students summarise Beowulf or Chaucer plot rather than analysing structure.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing for a course blog modelled on the JSTOR Daily site.

lessons.lesson_title: Resolve contested usage with style guides
lessons.learning_objective: I can resolve a usage question by consulting two style guides and citing them.
lessons.key_concepts: Style guides; usage debates; authority.
lessons.key_vocabulary: style guide, usage, authority, consult, cite
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students cite a website that disagrees with multiple major style guides.
lessons.real_world_hook: Settling a question about Oxford comma usage for a publication style sheet.

lessons.lesson_title: Initiate discussion on archaic texts
lessons.learning_objective: I can initiate and lead discussion on an archaic text with text-based questions.
lessons.key_concepts: Discussion on translation; structural questions; close reading.
lessons.key_vocabulary: initiate, archaic, translation, structural, close reading
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students avoid archaic texts in discussion and stay general.
lessons.real_world_hook: Leading a discussion like a host of an audiobook companion podcast.

lessons.lesson_title: Apply diction across registers
lessons.learning_objective: I can revise a paragraph to control diction across formal and creative registers.
lessons.key_concepts: Register; diction; consistency.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students mix archaic flourish with modern slang and call it style.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a podcast script for register fit with the show's brand.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze themes interacting in a tragedy
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how two or more themes interact in a Shakespearean tragedy.
lessons.key_concepts: Theme interaction; tragic structure; thematic counterpoint.
lessons.prerequisites: Tracking single theme in long form.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students keep themes parallel without exploring how they cut against each other.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing intersecting themes in a Best Picture-style prestige film.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze impact of choices on a play
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how an author's choices about how to develop and relate elements shape a tragedy.
lessons.key_concepts: Soliloquy, foil, structure; tragic mechanism.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students attribute tragedy to fate rather than to choices in the play.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing a tragic hero's choices like a critic on a film breakdown podcast.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze metaphysical conceit
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse a metaphysical conceit in a Donne or Marvell poem.
lessons.key_concepts: Conceit; extended metaphor; argument in verse.
lessons.key_vocabulary: conceit, extended metaphor, argument, paradox, witty
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat any extended metaphor as a conceit.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a Donne conceit to a viral analogy in a modern essay.

lessons.lesson_title: Write argument on tragic hero or conceit
lessons.learning_objective: I can write an argument essay on tragic hero or metaphysical conceit using textual evidence.
lessons.key_concepts: Argument from craft; balanced evidence; counterclaim.
lessons.key_vocabulary: tragic hero, conceit, evidence, counterclaim, claim
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students argue tragic hero status from one trait such as ambition only.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a piece like an analysis on a literary podcast's blog.

lessons.lesson_title: Use cumulative and periodic sentences
lessons.learning_objective: I can write cumulative and periodic sentences in analytic prose for effect.
lessons.key_concepts: Cumulative addition; periodic delay; rhetorical effect.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students cannot tell a cumulative sentence apart from a long string of fragments.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a graduation speech draft for memorable sentence shapes.

lessons.lesson_title: Demonstrate hortative, conditional, and subjunctive moods
lessons.learning_objective: I can use hortative, conditional, and subjunctive moods for effect in formal writing.
lessons.key_concepts: Verb mood in formal prose; advanced syntax.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students drop the subjunctive even in if-then constructions.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a model UN resolution where conditional clauses matter.

lessons.lesson_title: Participate in academic seminar on tragedy
lessons.learning_objective: I can participate in a structured seminar on tragedy with text-based questions and follow-up.
lessons.key_concepts: Seminar norms; reasoning chains; evidence ladder.
lessons.key_vocabulary: ladder, chain, follow up, anchor, evidence
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students offer opinion only and skip the anchoring quotation.
lessons.real_world_hook: Hosting a discussion like a guest on a literature podcast.

lessons.lesson_title: Take an AP-style timed essay on prose
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a 40-minute AP-style essay on a prose passage with thesis and support.
lessons.key_concepts: Timed essay; thesis on the fly; quick evidence selection.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students plan too long and never get to the third body paragraph.
lessons.real_world_hook: Drafting under timed conditions like an AP exam Q2 task.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze structure parts contributing to whole
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how structural choices in specific parts of a Romantic or Victorian novel contribute to overall meaning.
lessons.key_concepts: Volume and chapter design; serial publication context.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students forget that some Victorian novels appeared serially and were shaped by that.
lessons.real_world_hook: Analysing chapter design the way a season finale planner thinks about reveals.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze layered point of view including satire
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse a case where point of view requires distinguishing the stated from the meant.
lessons.key_concepts: Satire; free indirect discourse; layered voice.
lessons.key_vocabulary: satire, free indirect, layered, voice, irony
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students miss free indirect discourse and treat narration as flat.
lessons.real_world_hook: Reading an Austen chapter and a satirical newsletter for layered voice.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze multiple interpretations of a novel
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse multiple interpretations of a Romantic novel and evaluate each one.
lessons.key_concepts: Adaptation; performance; critical reception.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rank adaptations by fidelity to plot only.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing a Frankenstein adaptation on stage to a recent film version.

lessons.lesson_title: Write comparative analysis novel plus poetry
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a comparative analysis essay using a novel and a poem from the same period.
lessons.key_concepts: Comparative axis; period context; thematic linking.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students write two summaries side by side and call it comparison.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing a side-by-side analysis for a literary student journal.

lessons.lesson_title: Use cohesion across sections of long writing
lessons.learning_objective: I can use cohesion devices to link sections of a long essay across pages.
lessons.key_concepts: Long-form cohesion; recurrent threads; transitions.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students start each section as if it were standalone.
lessons.real_world_hook: Editing a research paper to read as one piece, not a stack of paragraphs.

lessons.lesson_title: Interpret figures of speech in context
lessons.learning_objective: I can interpret figures of speech in context, including pathetic fallacy and synecdoche.
lessons.key_concepts: Pathetic fallacy; synecdoche; context-dependent meaning.
lessons.key_vocabulary: pathetic fallacy, synecdoche, context, interpret, figure
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students label pathetic fallacy as personification and stop.
lessons.real_world_hook: Annotating a Wordsworth poem on the Poetry Foundation site.

lessons.lesson_title: Take AP-style timed essay on poetry
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a 40-minute AP-style essay on a poem with thesis and support.
lessons.key_concepts: Timed poetry essay; quick close reading; evidence selection.
lessons.key_vocabulary: timed, poem, AP, thesis, close reading
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students paraphrase the poem instead of analysing it.
lessons.real_world_hook: Drafting under timed conditions like an AP exam Q1 task.

lessons.lesson_title: Adapt speech to varied audiences
lessons.learning_objective: I can deliver the same analysis adapted to peer, professional, and general public audiences.
lessons.key_concepts: Audience adaptation; register; example choice.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students translate vocabulary only and not register or examples.
lessons.real_world_hook: Pitching the same idea on a school podcast and on a teacher's panel.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze point of view in postcolonial fiction
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how a postcolonial work draws on and transforms its sources.
lessons.key_concepts: Postcolonial response; rewriting; counter-narrative.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students treat a counter-narrative as just a different story.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing Achebe on Heart of Darkness as a counter-narrative discussion.

lessons.lesson_title: Analyze themes interacting across two works
lessons.learning_objective: I can analyse how themes interact across two works from different traditions.
lessons.key_concepts: Cross-tradition themes; comparative reading.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students see themes as the same when traditions are different.
lessons.real_world_hook: Comparing themes in a modernist British novel and a postcolonial African novel.

lessons.lesson_title: Integrate sources across media for research
lessons.learning_objective: I can integrate multiple sources of information across media to address a research question.
lessons.key_concepts: Multi-media research; synthesis; balanced sources.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students rely heavily on one media type for convenience.
lessons.real_world_hook: Producing a backgrounder like a major newsroom's explainer team.

lessons.lesson_title: Conduct capstone research with depth
lessons.learning_objective: I can plan and conduct a capstone research project of 3000 to 4000 words across two periods or traditions.
lessons.key_concepts: Capstone planning; iteration; controlling claim.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students plan a question they cannot finish in the available time.
lessons.real_world_hook: Producing a capstone like an undergraduate thesis preview.

lessons.lesson_title: Synthesise sources for capstone argument
lessons.learning_objective: I can synthesise multiple authoritative sources into a coherent capstone argument.
lessons.key_concepts: Synthesis at scale; quality of evidence; integration.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students assemble sources and never integrate them.
lessons.real_world_hook: Writing like a long-form Atlantic feature.

lessons.lesson_title: Write a college admissions essay with reflection
lessons.learning_objective: I can write a college admissions essay that reflects on a specific moment with voice and reflection.
lessons.key_concepts: Personal essay; voice; reflection at the close.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students choose a worthy topic and skip the actual scene.
lessons.real_world_hook: Drafting an essay for a real Common App prompt before fall applications.

lessons.lesson_title: Edit for advanced conventions and clarity
lessons.learning_objective: I can edit a capstone draft for advanced conventions, varied syntax, and clarity.
lessons.key_concepts: Final editing pass; advanced conventions; clarity.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students proofread only the first and last pages of a long paper.
lessons.real_world_hook: Filing copy as a freelance writer would for final publication.

lessons.lesson_title: Defend a senior portfolio orally
lessons.learning_objective: I can present and defend a senior portfolio with three to five anchor pieces in a 10-minute exhibition.
lessons.key_concepts: Portfolio defence; reasoning chain; reflection.
lessons.common_misconceptions: Students present polished work without explaining how it shows growth.
lessons.real_world_hook: Defending a portfolio like a senior project at a model school exhibition night.

practices.what_students_do: Students read a passage slowly, mark patterns, and reread with a focused question. They annotate diction, syntax, structure, and figurative language.
practices.implications: Each unit includes at least one close-reading lesson; teachers model with a think-aloud.

practices.what_students_do: Students select the strongest evidence, quote or paraphrase accurately, and integrate it with signal phrases.
practices.implications: Evidence quality, not quantity, is graded on every analytic task; rubrics distinguish strong from sufficient.

practices.what_students_do: Students explain how authorial choices about word, sentence, paragraph, and overall structure shape meaning.
practices.implications: Every literary unit ends with an analytic task on craft, not on plot recall.

practices.what_students_do: Students delineate a writer's claim, reasons, and evidence, then judge validity, relevance, and sufficiency.
practices.implications: Argument evaluation appears in literary, informational, and spoken contexts every year.

practices.what_students_do: Students take a position, develop reasons, gather evidence, and address counterclaims fairly.
practices.implications: Every grade writes a sustained argument; later grades add formal style and synthesis.

practices.what_students_do: Students locate sources, judge credibility, take notes, paraphrase, and cite using MLA basics.
practices.implications: Source evaluation is taught explicitly, not assumed; lateral reading is modeled.

practices.what_students_do: Students revise for structure and evidence and edit for syntax and conventions.
practices.implications: Process writing is required for all major pieces; revision is graded separately from drafting.

practices.what_students_do: Students prepare with evidence, build on others' ideas, and probe reasoning.
practices.implications: Socratic seminars and structured discussion appear at every grade; protocols are taught.

practices.what_students_do: Students present claims and findings clearly and listen to evaluate a speaker's logic and rhetoric.
practices.implications: Each year includes at least one formal presentation graded with a rubric.

practices.practice: Using grammar and conventions in context
practices.what_students_do: Students apply grammar choices for clarity and effect, not as isolated drills.
practices.implications: Grammar is taught inside writing units; mini-lessons connect to current drafts.

misconceptions.misconception: Students give a one-word topic (friendship, love) and call it a theme.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Curriculum often introduces theme through topic prompts; students learn to label, not to claim.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the author saying about this topic? Look for the sentence-level theme statement.
misconceptions.remediation: Use a sentence frame: The author suggests that ____. Practice across short texts before novels.

misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the narrator's view as the author's view.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Younger texts often use a first-person narrator who shares author values, so students overgeneralise.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: does the author endorse this narrator, or is there distance? Look for unreliable narration cues.
misconceptions.remediation: Pair an unreliable narrator with a critical essay so students can hear the gap.

misconceptions.misconception: Students write plot summary and label it analysis.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Summary is easier and is often praised in elementary grades.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what does this paragraph claim, and what evidence supports it? Underline claims, separate from retelling.
misconceptions.remediation: Require a verb of analysis (argues, suggests, complicates) in each topic sentence.

misconceptions.misconception: Students write a strong feeling and call it an argument.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Argument and opinion writing are taught together in earlier grades.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the claim, and what reasons could change a thoughtful person's mind?
misconceptions.remediation: Teach the claim-reason-evidence triplet explicitly; ban I think in argument drafts.

misconceptions.misconception: Students confuse tone (author) with mood (reader feeling).
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Both terms get introduced together and use similar adjective lists.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: whose feeling is this, the writer's or mine? Find diction that creates tone.
misconceptions.remediation: Use a two-column chart: tone evidence vs mood evidence on the same passage.

misconceptions.misconception: Students treat dictionary meanings as the whole story.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Vocabulary tests reward denotation; classroom reading often does not surface connotation.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what feelings or associations does this word carry? Compare close synonyms.
misconceptions.remediation: Use synonym ladders (slim, thin, gaunt) and discuss why an author chose one.

misconceptions.misconception: Students predict an outcome and call that foreshadowing.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Prediction is taught as a comprehension strategy and looks similar from the outside.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: where in the text did the author plant this clue? Mark the planted detail.
misconceptions.remediation: Require students to underline the textual clue when they claim foreshadowing.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label any repeated image as a theme.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Motif is sometimes introduced without contrast to theme.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: is this a recurring pattern (motif) or a claim about life (theme)? Both can coexist.
misconceptions.remediation: Use a motif log alongside a theme statement to keep both visible.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label every object as a symbol.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Once symbol is taught, students overapply it.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: does the text show this object carrying meaning beyond itself, repeatedly?
misconceptions.remediation: Require three pieces of textual evidence to claim a symbol.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label all credentials ethos and miss tone-based ethos.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Ethos is introduced via Aristotle as credibility, which sounds like resume.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: how does the speaker build trust through tone, fairness, and shared values?
misconceptions.remediation: Compare two speakers with similar credentials but different rhetorical ethos.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label any emotional content pathos without checking purpose.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Pathos is often defined as emotion without nuance.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: how is this emotional appeal meant to move the audience toward the claim?
misconceptions.remediation: Require students to link pathos to a specific claim in the speech.

misconceptions.misconception: Students think a paragraph with numbers automatically has strong logos.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Data-rich texts get called logical even when reasoning is weak.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: are the data relevant to the claim, and does the reasoning hold up?
misconceptions.remediation: Audit a data-heavy paragraph for non sequiturs and unsupported leaps.

misconceptions.misconception: Students name the easiest opposing view and dismiss it.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Curricula sometimes treat counterclaim as a checklist box.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the strongest version of the opposing view, and how would you address it?
misconceptions.remediation: Require steelmanning: have students write the counterclaim before they argue.

misconceptions.topic_area: Plagiarism as copy and paste only
misconceptions.misconception: Students think paraphrase without citation is acceptable.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Plagiarism instruction often focuses on quotation only.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: is this idea or wording mine, and have I cited the source?
misconceptions.remediation: Teach paraphrase quality and citation as one lesson, not two separate ones.

misconceptions.misconception: Students dismiss Wikipedia entirely.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Earlier grades taught it as off-limits; the reasoning was not updated.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what does Wikipedia's footnote chain show about evidence?
misconceptions.remediation: Use Wikipedia as a launchpad; require lateral reading on cited sources.

misconceptions.misconception: Students avoid passive voice everywhere.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Grammar checkers flag it indiscriminately.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: who is the actor, and does it matter? Passive may be correct in science or news.
misconceptions.remediation: Compare lab reports and op-eds for appropriate passive vs active voice.

misconceptions.misconception: Students bury claims in long, tangled sentences.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Academic models include long sentences, which get imitated without control.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: can a reader find the subject and verb? Is each clause earning its place?
misconceptions.remediation: Require subject-verb proximity check on every paragraph.

misconceptions.misconception: Students never use fragments, even when deliberate.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Earlier grades drilled fragment correction.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: is this fragment intentional and does it work for the audience?
misconceptions.remediation: Read examples from professional essays that use fragments effectively.

misconceptions.topic_area: Thesis at end of intro only
misconceptions.misconception: Students place the thesis only in the last sentence of the intro.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: A formula was taught as if it were the only structure.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: does the placement serve the argument and the reader?
misconceptions.remediation: Read columns and essays that locate the thesis early, late, or returning.

misconceptions.misconception: Students treat the five-paragraph essay as the highest form.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Test prep practices the form repeatedly.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: does your structure serve your claim, or vice versa?
misconceptions.remediation: Have students restructure a five-paragraph essay into a stronger shape.

misconceptions.misconception: Students assume they cannot understand Shakespeare without a translation.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Some classroom practices use modern paraphrase first.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what can you understand from staging, context, and pattern before glossing?
misconceptions.remediation: Start with a short scene read aloud, then layer in close reading.

misconceptions.misconception: Students assume non-rhyming poems are not real poems.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Earlier exposure favours rhyme-driven verse.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the form, and what does it do?
misconceptions.remediation: Compare a rhyming poem and a free verse poem on the same theme.

misconceptions.misconception: Students reread without a focus.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Close reading was introduced without a stance.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what question are you reading for this time?
misconceptions.remediation: Provide a focus question for each rereading pass.

misconceptions.misconception: Students label any sharpness as irony.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Sarcasm is the most familiar form.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the gap between what is stated and what is meant or known?
misconceptions.remediation: Distinguish verbal, situational, and dramatic irony with current examples.

misconceptions.misconception: Students write arguments in an outraged tone.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Comments sections model heat over clarity.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what tone will most likely persuade your audience?
misconceptions.remediation: Have students rewrite a strong argument in a calmer register and compare effect.

misconceptions.misconception: Students rely heavily on a single source.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Earlier research projects required only one or two sources.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: who else is talking about this, and where do they disagree?
misconceptions.remediation: Require triangulation: at least three independent sources for major claims.

misconceptions.misconception: Students dismiss a source as biased without evaluating evidence.
misconceptions.why_it_happens: Media literacy slogans simplify bias.
misconceptions.diagnostic_approach: Ask: what is the perspective, and what evidence is offered?
misconceptions.remediation: Compare opinion and reporting from the same outlet on the same story.

glossary.definition: A brief reference to a person, place, event, or text outside the work.
A character or force that opposes the protagonist.
A novel that traces a protagonist's growth from youth to maturity.
The methods an author uses to develop a character (direct or indirect).
The point of highest tension in a plot, after which the action turns.
The struggle between opposing forces in a narrative, internal or external.
A gap between what a character knows and what the audience knows.
A character who undergoes significant internal change.
A long narrative poem on heroic subjects, often involving a journey.
Introductory information about characters, setting, and prior events.
The events after the climax that move toward resolution.
A scene set earlier than the main story line.
A character whose qualities contrast with another to highlight traits.
Hints in earlier text that point toward later events.
A story that contains another story or set of stories inside it.
Narration that blends a character's voice with the narrator's.
An archetype where a protagonist departs, faces trials, and returns transformed.
Deliberate exaggeration for effect.
Language that appeals to the senses to create mental pictures.
Beginning a narrative in the middle of the action.
A gap between what is said or expected and what is meant or occurs.
A direct comparison without like or as.
A recurring image, idea, or pattern in a text.
The voice that tells a story; not always the same as the author.
A figure that joins two opposite terms (deafening silence).
A statement that seems contradictory but reveals a truth.
Giving human qualities to nonhuman things.
The arrangement of events in a narrative.
The vantage point from which a story is told (first, third limited, third omniscient).
The central character whose actions drive the narrative.
The settling of conflicts at the end of a narrative.
Events that build tension after the exposition.
The time, place, and social context of a story.
A comparison using like or as.
A speech in which a character on stage speaks alone to reveal thoughts.
A 14-line poem in iambic pentameter, often with a turn (volta).
A group of lines forming a unit in a poem.
A character who does not undergo significant internal change.
A narrative mode that follows continuous thought.
An object, image, or action that stands for something beyond itself.
A central idea or claim about life that a text develops.
The author's attitude toward subject or audience, conveyed through diction and syntax.
A protagonist of high standing whose flaw or error leads to downfall.
A narrator whose credibility is compromised.
The turn in a sonnet where thought or argument shifts.
Repetition of the same word or phrase at the start of successive clauses.
Juxtaposition of contrasting ideas in balanced phrases.
Omission of conjunctions for compression or speed.
A balanced structure with reversed order (ask not what your country can do for you).
An appeal based on the speaker's credibility and character.
Appeal to the right moment or timely opportunity.
Understatement using a negation of the opposite (not bad).
An appeal based on reason, evidence, and logic.
Substituting a related term for another (the crown for the king).
Using matching grammatical forms for paired or listed items.
An appeal to the audience's emotions or values.
Repeated use of conjunctions for emphasis (and...and...and).
A question asked for effect, not for an answer.
Substituting a part for the whole or whole for part (all hands on deck).
Deliberately presenting something as less significant than it is.
A construction where the subject performs the action.
A word that modifies a noun.
A word that modifies a verb, adjective, or other adverb.
The noun a pronoun refers to.
A noun phrase that renames an adjacent noun.
A group of words containing a subject and predicate.
A word that joins equal grammatical elements (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
A modifier with no clear referent in the sentence.
A clause that cannot stand alone as a sentence.
A verb form ending in -ing used as a noun.
A clause that can stand alone as a sentence.
The base form of a verb, usually preceded by to.
A word, phrase, or clause that describes another element.
Turning a verb or adjective into a noun (decide becomes decision).
A verb form used as an adjective or in verb phrases.
